clue.text: Not quite grade-A, but our little George is present, that is, and they're mainly concerned with property values.

definitions.text: they're mainly concerned with property values
definitions.note: a collective noun for a class of people, so it takes 'they'

parts.note: B is the grade just below an A, so a mark that falls short of top grade
taken as written
Geo is the short form of the name George
taken as written

explanation.surface: A family note: young George has earned only a B, and the household frets about the price of their house.
explanation.walkthrough: IE is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for 'that is'. 'Property values' hints at the middle class's attachment to owning things.
explanation.definitionFit: The middle class, in Marxist and everyday usage, is the propertied class whose values centre on ownership and respectability.

clue.text: Finished pale and wan–or just too much removed?

definitions.note: said of a bank account from which more has been taken out than was in it

parts.note: over means at an end, done
a drawn face is tired, haggard and pale

explanation.surface: Someone looking exhausted and pallid asks whether they are merely finished or have pushed things too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removed' looks like distance or detachment, but here it means money withdrawn from a bank account.
explanation.definitionFit: An overdrawn account has had more money withdrawn than it held, so too much has been taken out.

clue.text: Do his tales explain natural history? Just so!

definitions.text: Do his tales explain natural history? Just so!

parts.words: Do his tales explain natural history?
parts.note: the author's children's stories explain how animals got their features, such as the leopard's spots
read as 'exactly right', but also the title of his collection, the Just So Stories

explanation.walkthrough: 'Just so!' looks like an emphatic yes to the question; it is the title of the book in question.
explanation.definitionFit: The English writer published Just So Stories (1902), fables explaining how the camel got its hump and the elephant its trunk.

clue.text: See 8
It's chic, as I hear this puzzle is, to ensure that something is not left out.

definitions.text: ensure that something is not left out

parts.note: something chic is fashionable, or in

indicators.note: the setter is listening, so the word clued is taken by how it sounds rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: every crossword is clued: its answers are given clues

explanation.surface: The setter boasts that the puzzle is stylish and carefully made so that nothing has been forgotten.
explanation.definitionFit: To include something is to make it part of a whole, so that it is counted in rather than omitted.

clue.text: One fateful day? To Little Albert, it's perfect!

parts.note: the Ides of March was the day Julius Caesar was murdered; one day of the Ides, made singular, is taken as Ide
Al is the short form of the name Albert

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a certain date was doomed; young Albert cheerfully pronounces it perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter treats the Ides, a plural word naming a single day, as if it had a singular Ide.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideal as an adjective means exactly as one would wish, without flaw.

clue.text: Mr. Sawyer, pet, is to sleep with lots of women.

definitions.note: the answer as a verb: to tomcat (around)

parts.note: Tom Sawyer, the boy hero of Mark Twain's novel
a cat is a household pet

explanation.surface: A scandalous suggestion that Twain's boy hero, or perhaps someone's pet, is a philanderer.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an American slang verb, it means to chase women promiscuously, as a roaming male cat seeks mates.

clue.text: The head of the synagogue starts to cry, but they really get the picture!

parts.note: a rabbi leads a Jewish congregation
someone who tears up begins to cry, so tears stands for crying

explanation.surface: A rabbi breaks down weeping, while someone else, unmoved, understands the situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get the picture' sounds like understanding; it is literal, about a television signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabbit ears are the V-shaped indoor television aerial that picks up a broadcast signal, named for their shape.

clue.text: Do a little sparring with an important member of the church. (Might look good in your yard!)

definitions.text: Might look good in your yard

parts.note: sparring is practice boxing, so to box

parts.words: an important member of the church
parts.note: an elder is a senior lay officer of a church

explanation.surface: A church elder squaring up for a friendly bout, with an aside about garden ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: Yard is the American word for a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: The box elder is a North American maple often planted as a shade tree in gardens.

clue.text: The salad gets et, too, by the sound of it–just as he said, finally.

definitions.text: The salad gets et, too, by the sound of it–just as he said, finally.

parts.note: a famous salad of romaine lettuce, croutons and parmesan bears this name

parts.words: gets et, too, by the sound of it
parts.note: 'et too' sounds like 'et tu', and et is also old slang for eaten
'Et tu, Brute?' are given by Shakespeare as the dying general's last words

explanation.walkthrough: The salad is eaten ('et') too, which sounds like the reproach the Roman general spoke to Brutus as he was stabbed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman dictator's name is shared by the classic salad, and 'Et tu, Brute?' is his famous dying line.

clue.text: An ill-bred man–a Scot–but from a French colony.

parts.note: the indefinite article gives the letter A
a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably
Ian is a typically Scottish first name, standing for any Scotsman

explanation.surface: A disparaging remark about a rude Scotsman who turns out to come from somewhere French.
explanation.definitionFit: Acadia was the French colony in what is now Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; its people were Acadians.

clue.text: It's supposed to put the little one to sleep, with a little quiet when the baby doesn't start to make it.

definitions.text: It's supposed to put the little one to sleep

parts.note: a lull is a brief spell of calm

indicators.note: the baby loses its first letter, the one it would start with

parts.note: the word taken as written, before it loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A parent explains how to soothe an infant to sleep in the brief calm when it stops fussing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cradle song is sung softly to soothe a young child into sleep.

clue.text: Africa dream reveals the nucleus of the group.

indicators.note: the run of letters across the two words shows the answer, sitting inside them

parts.note: the words as written, with the answer running across their join

explanation.surface: A dream about Africa uncovers the central core of some organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadre is a core of trained people around whom a larger organisation or party is built.

clue.text: Leave someone ashore with a few pearls, for instance.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to maroon, leave stuck on the shore
second meaning: a string of beads or pearls

explanation.surface: A castaway left on the beach, perhaps clutching a small necklace.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to leave someone stranded or marooned; the noun is a single string or thread, as of pearls.

clue.text: A real top type–right? Gets sort of beat–and embittered!

parts.note: an ace is someone at the very top of their field

indicators.note: only a sort of version of the word beat, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A champion, sort of beaten, ends up bitter about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is used here as an old adjective meaning soured, as in Webster's, not just the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin acerbus, sour or harsh; as an adjective it describes someone made bitter or exasperated.

clue.text: Byzantine cabal comes together by volcanic flow to make a covering that might be used in a stickup.

definitions.text: a covering that might be used in a stickup

indicators.note: Byzantine means intricately tangled, so the letters of cabal are worked into a complicated new order

parts.note: the word taken as written; a cabal is a secret clique of plotters
lava is molten rock flowing from a volcano

explanation.surface: A scheming clique meets near a lava flow and plots an armed robbery.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted hood covering the head and face except for the eyes, worn by robbers to hide their identity.

clue.text: Turn around and around with the rest shook up–just like a little old lady nobody wanted!

definitions.text: a little old lady nobody wanted

parts.note: to spin is to rotate repeatedly

indicators.note: the word rest is shaken about, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sad scene of whirling about until everything else is unsettled, ending with a lonely old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The old-fashioned term for an unmarried older woman, with the dated assumption that no suitor wanted her.

clue.text: "I'm on this!" means you've lost power.

definitions.text: "I'm on this!" means you've lost power.

parts.note: sounds like someone taking charge, but asks the solver to put I'M on the front of the answer
with I'M in front, the answer becomes a word for powerless, so the answer itself means powerful

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is never defined directly: adding I'M at the front makes the word meaning without power, so the answer must be its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means strong or forceful, and prefixing the letters im- reverses that sense to weakness.

clue.text: Square on the justification you'll find a crime against this magazine, or so it sounds.

definitions.text: a crime against this magazine, or so it sounds
definitions.note: the puzzle ran in The Nation, and the crime is betrayal of one's nation

parts.note: a T-square, the drafting tool, gives the letter T
a reason is the justification for doing something

explanation.surface: A boast that, given good grounds, you'll uncover an offence against the magazine in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This magazine' is The Nation, where the puzzle appeared, so the definition is a pun on 'crime against the nation'.
explanation.definitionFit: Betraying one's country, by aiding its enemies or plotting against the state, is the crime known by this name.

clue.text: Associated with trees, poetically…

parts.note: looks like a description such as sylvan, but points to a person linked with trees
the link is a poem

explanation.walkthrough: 'Poetically' suggests a literary adjective for woodland; it is the surname of the poet of 'Trees'.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce Kilmer wrote the 1913 poem beginning 'I think that I shall never see / A poem lovely as a tree.'

clue.text: See 3
One of 4 on the upcoming study made money.

parts.note: 4 down is EARS, so one of them is a single ear

indicators.note: in a down clue the word for study is read rising, from bottom to top

parts.note: a den is a private study or workroom

explanation.surface: Someone working on the next study pocketed some cash.
explanation.definitionFit: To have earned is to have gained money in return for work.

clue.text: …with what's left of the tree going to the news boss, in short–not knowing the answer.

parts.note: the stump is what remains after a tree is felled
ed is short for editor, the boss of a newspaper

explanation.surface: Continuing from the trees, a felled trunk is sent to the editor, who is baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses carry on from the clue before, which was about trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stumped means being baffled by a question and unable to give a reply.

clue.text: Count this–it means I won't join!

definitions.text: Count this–it means I won't join!

parts.note: the answer completes the phrase begun by the word count
the full phrase is how someone declines to take part

explanation.walkthrough: Put 'count' before the answer to get the idiom refusing to take part.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'count me out' is the idiomatic way to decline an invitation or opt out of a plan.

clue.text: A classic tale on the broken-up street in Paris–to find a person of taste.

parts.note: an epic is a long classic narrative such as the Iliad

indicators.note: the word for street is broken up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: rue is French for street

explanation.surface: A literary find among the ruins of a Parisian street, made by someone discerning.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicure is a connoisseur with refined taste in food and drink.

clue.text: Charge me subjectively–it takes me where I want to go.

definitions.text: it takes me where I want to go

parts.note: to tax is to impose a charge
I is the subject form of the pronoun me

explanation.surface: A passenger muses that the vehicle charging a fare carries them where they choose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subjectively' is grammar: the subject case of 'me' is 'I'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab for hire drives a passenger to the destination of their choosing.

clue.text: The sort of sting has nothing but bars associated with them.

definitions.note: the answer is plural, the bars themselves; 'associated with them' completes the surface

indicators.note: a sort of sting is a rearranged version of the word, so its letters are shuffled

parts.note: the word taken as written, as the letters to rearrange
O is the round shape of zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A police sting operation leading to nothing but prison bars for those caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests prison after a sting; it means metal cast in blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingots are blocks of cast metal, especially gold or silver, commonly called bars.

clue.text: Possibly the main date would be fixed up in cartoon fashion.

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for the adjective, as in drawn and moving like a cartoon

indicators.note: signals that the words may be some other arrangement of the same letters
the main date is fixed up, so its letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the words taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An important appointment gets rearranged into something out of a comic strip.
explanation.definitionFit: Animated films are cartoons, made from drawings shown in sequence to create movement.

clue.text: Refusing any change, running for office like little Mr. Henry.

parts.note: to stand is to be a candidate in an election
Pat is short for Patrick, as in Patrick Henry, the American revolutionary orator

explanation.surface: A candidate in an election stubbornly refuses to budge, much like Patrick Henry.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand pat is a poker-derived idiom for keeping one's position and resisting any alteration.
